Lithuania
lith-oo-AY-nee-a
n. (the grand duchy whose Reformation gave the Lithuanian language its first printed book in 1547)
Latin Lituania; Lithuanian Lietuva. The tongue is the most archaic surviving Indo-European language of Europe.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Lithuania is the grand duchy in which the Reformation created a written language. The last pagan state in Europe, baptised only in 1387, it was joined to Poland and ruled by a magnate class whose greatest house, the Radziwills, went Reformed and endowed churches, presses and schools; Mikolajus Radvila the Black paid for the Brest Bible in Polish in 1563. The work that lasted was in Lithuanian. Abraomas Kulvietis founded a school at Vilnius in 1539 and was driven out; Martynas Mazvydas, trained at Konigsberg, published there in 1547 the Catechismusa prasty szadei, the first book ever printed in Lithuanian, a catechism with a rhymed preface and hymns, addressed to a people whose priests mostly could not preach to them; Baltramiejus Vilentas followed with a translation of the Gospels and Epistles, and Jonas Bretkunas translated the whole Bible into Lithuanian by 1590, though it was never printed. Kedainiai became the chief Reformed centre under Radziwill patronage. The Counter-Reformation recovered the magnates and with them the duchy. The dictionary enters Lithuania because its first printed book was a catechism, which is to say that the nation's literature begins with an attempt to teach peasants the faith in words they used.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a catechism as instruction by question and answer; a preface as something spoken introductory; pagan as heathen, not Christian; and a grand duchy as the territory of a grand duke.

expand to see more

CATECHISM, n. A form of instruction by means of questions and answers, particularly in the principles of religion.

PREFACE, n. Something spoken as introductory to a discourse, or written as introductory to a book.

PAGAN, n. A heathen; a Gentile; one who worships false gods; one not a Christian, Jew or Mahometan.

GRAND DUCHY, n. The territory or dominions of a grand duke.

RHYME, n. In poetry, a correspondence of sound in the terminating words or syllables of two verses.

Key Scripture

Act 2:8 — "And how hear we every man in our own tongue, wherein we were born?"

Mat 28:19 — "Go ye therefore, and teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost:"

Isa 42:6 — "I the LORD have called thee in righteousness, and will hold thine hand, and will keep thee, and give thee for a covenant of the people, for a light of the Gentiles;"

Act 26:18 — "To open their eyes, and to turn them from darkness to light, and from the power of Satan unto God, that they may receive forgiveness of sins, and inheritance among them which are sanctified by faith that is in me."

Modern Corruption

Grand duchy, pagan until 1387, whose Reformation produced the first printed Lithuanian book in 1547 and a complete Lithuanian Bible by 1590.

expand to see more

The corruption to be named is the baptism of a nation without the teaching of it. Lithuania was declared Christian in 1387 by its grand duke's decision, and a century and a half later its people had no book, no catechism and often no preaching in their language; the old gods were still named in the villages. Mazvydas's preface of 1547 says as much in verse, calling his countrymen to leave what their fathers served and to come and read. The commission is to teach and not merely to baptise: “Go ye therefore, and teach all nations, baptizing them” (Mat 28:19) puts the instruction first in the order of the sentence and the work.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that conversion is from darkness and must be understood to be real. The apostle's charge was to open men's eyes and “to turn them from darkness to light, and from the power of Satan unto God” (Act 26:18), which cannot be done by a prince's edict. The servant of the Lord is given “for a light of the Gentiles” (Isa 42:6), and the gift at Pentecost answers how: that each man hears “in our own tongue, wherein we were born” (Act 2:8), which in 1547 meant a printed Lithuanian catechism.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek matheteuo (G3100), to make disciples; Greek skotos (G4655), darkness; Greek dialektos (G1258), the speech of a region.

expand to see more

Greek matheteuo (G3100) — to make a disciple, to teach; “Go ye therefore, and teach all nations”, Matthew 28:19.

Greek baptizo (G907) — to baptize, to wash; “baptizing them in the name of the Father”, Matthew 28:19.

Greek skotos (G4655) — darkness, both natural and moral; “to turn them from darkness to light”, Acts 26:18.

Hebrew or (H216) — light; “for a light of the Gentiles”, Isaiah 42:6.

Greek dialektos (G1258) — the speech of a region; “in our own tongue, wherein we were born”, Acts 2:8.

Usage

"“Go ye therefore, and teach all nations, baptizing them” (Mat 28:19) — a nation baptised by edict in 1387 and untaught."

"“in our own tongue, wherein we were born” (Act 2:8) — Mazvydas's Lithuanian catechism, Konigsberg 1547."

"“to turn them from darkness to light, and from the power of Satan unto God” (Act 26:18) — the old gods still named in the villages."
